fullText:
Most families of the six soldiers killed in the deadliest attack of the Iran war were not attending a major White House event for Gold Star families hosted by President Donald Trump.

Only one family member of those killed in an Iranian drone strike March 1 on Port Shuaiba in Kuwait confirmed to The Associated Press that they planned to attend Tuesday's reception with Trump and the first lady. Troops who survived the attack have raised questions about why they were stationed at a site that didn't have sufficient air protection and was viewed as a likely target.

The war, launched Feb. 28, has claimed the lives of 19 U.S. troops and wounded more than 800 others. The annual gathering honors Gold Star Mother's and Family's Day, which falls on the last weekend of September.

The White House said this year's reception honors nearly 40 fallen service members from conflicts dating to the Vietnam War. Trump was expected to deliver remarks followed by a candle-lighting ceremony and a musical performance that included a rendition of "America the Beautiful."

Gold Star families have expressed frustration over the lack of information from the Pentagon about the strike in Kuwait.

"There are questions about what happened before the attack, what information was available, what decisions were made, and what happened in the moments leading up to six American soldiers losing their lives," Joey Amor — whose 39-year-old wife, Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor, was among those killed — said in a public Facebook statement Monday. "I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency."

U.S. soldiers wounded in the attack told the AP of the unheeded concerns they raised about the threat and that the military medical system failed them in the weeks that followed. The AP's account of the March 1 attack is based on interviews with 13 soldiers.

The Army declined to comment on the AP's reporting on the Port Shuaiba strike, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack, which was completed in June. The Army has said it is still redacting sensitive information before releasing the findings. The Pentagon also declined to comment.

Honoring soldiers who died in combat can be a powerful recognition of their service that cuts across politics, said John Thompson, a former Army sergeant and founder of Salute to the Fallen, an Iowa organization that supports veteran mental health, suicide prevention and funeral expenses.

He said several families told him they could not go because they did not receive enough notice about the event.

The White House began sending out invitations to Gold Star families — the military's designation for relatives of troops killed while on active duty — about two weeks ago, according to several families who said they received phone calls and emailed invitations.

"What they've told me is there has been a lot of confusion around this event, and they weren't given the details in time," Thompson said, adding that some were also not in a position to pay for the trip.

At least two said they did not receive an invite, though there can be hurdles to tracking down families' personal information.

Some Gold Star families say they are grateful for how the Trump administration and military have honored their loved one's sacrifice. Other families say the way the White House has handled the reception is the latest indication that the administration does not respect the price they have paid.

In the early days of the war, Trump described it as a "little excursion." On Sept. 4, he called the conflict "small potatoes."

The widow of Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan, who died in the March 1 attack, said she and her two children were not invited.

Tina Marzan said that in the immediate aftermath of her husband's death, she told federal officials she did not want to be contacted after receiving multiple calls. But she had hoped they would have tried to reach her or others in her family for an event like this, she said.

"We should be there," Tina Marzan told the AP. "I mean, that's not a question."

The White House said it does not contact people who request not to be contacted.

Some family members of soldiers who were killed in the war have not taken issue with Trump's remarks.

Donna Burhans, the mother of Maj. Cody Khork, who was one of those killed at Port Shuaiba, said she did not receive an invitation but would not have attended because it's too painful. She has described herself as a "big fan" of Trump after meeting him during the dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base.

"I just can't keep going thru (sic) this over and over," she told the AP in a text message.

The White House said it attempted to send invitations to Khork's family members.

The spouse of Maj. Alex Klinner, an airman who was killed in an Iran-related combat operation this summer, said receiving less than two weeks' notice did not give her enough time to arrange for overnight care for her three young children.

In a text message, Libby Klinner said she would not have gone anyway, adding, "I have no interest in supporting an administration that has been so reckless with the lives of our service members."

Brook reported from New Orleans, and Watson from San Diego. Associated Press writers Allen G. Breed in Wake Forest, North Carolina, Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report.

title: This Lawsuit Could Make Big Oil Pay for the Harm It’s Caused
description: Elie...
fullText:
The question is whether the Supreme Court will let it.

The Supreme Court began its new term on Monday by hearing oral arguments in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. The case involves a potentially landmark environmental lawsuit filed by the city of Boulder, Colorado, against two major fossil fuel industry polluters. The suit is modeled after old lawsuits against the tobacco industry: Boulder alleges that Suncor and ExxonMobil used deceptive marketing practices to sell products that have caused climate change and harmed the city, and it is now seeking damages for those harms.

Monday’s hearing wasn’t actually about those harms but whether the lawsuit should survive a motion to dismiss. If it does, it could allow local governments and maybe even individual citizens to sue energy companies for the effects of climate change. People might be able to sue for everything from adverse health outcomes to lost property. It could fundamentally change the way oil and gas companies operate across the country and, most likely, across the entire world.

But the lawsuit is not going to be successful. Unlike the tobacco industry—or the asbestos industry or opioid manufacturers or any other industry at the center of groundbreaking mass tort litigation—this is Big Oil we’re talking about, an industry with a market valuation upwards of $4 trillion. It’s like Spider-Man going from fighting the guys who stuck up a 7-11 to fighting an intergalactic alien invasion in one movie. There is no way this court is going to let local tort litigation regulate the global production and consumption of energy and its effects on the 8.2 billion people living on this planet.

The challenge is that while many of the justices don’t want Boulder to win as a practical matter, most of them are not quite sure when and how Boulder should lose as a legal matter. Monday’s Supreme Court arguments were messy because there are many competing ideas about whether the Supreme Court should kill the case now, kill it later, or wait and hope it dies on its own.

The case arrived in front of the Supreme Court on appeal from the Colorado State Supreme Court, which ruled that the lawsuit could survive a motion to dismiss by the fossil fuel companies and head to trial in Colorado. That presents the first problem for the Supreme Court, because it’s unclear if the court should have jurisdiction to hear this appeal at all, or if it should wait for the Colorado courts to do their work and then review their decision.

Justice Clarence Thomas questioned the lawyer for the energy companies, Kannon Shanmugam, and Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris (the Trump administration is on the side of the fossil fuel industry, which should surprise no one) about this very point. Two of the liberal justices, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, suggested that the Supreme Court should wait until the Colorado proceedings have finished, though Kagan gave pretty strong indications that Boulder should lose in state court.

The energy companies, of course, do not want to be dragged through state court. Shanmugam argued that if the Supreme Court allows the Boulder litigation to go forward, the very next day his energy clients will be sued by a veritable horde of municipalities and states. The cost of litigation is not normally something the Supreme Court should consider, but Shanmugam argued that his clients needed an answer to whether these suits should be allowed now, not years from now when the companies have been sued by every local district attorney looking for a good headline.

Instead, Shanmugam argued that Boulder’s lawsuit should be preempted by federal law: Preemption is the general principle that state law cannot be applied to an area where federal law has already spoken. The energy companies say that the Clean Air Act and the “structure of the Constitution” prevents states from regulating air pollution. They argue that since air pollution somewhat obviously and easily crosses state lines, and since climate change literally affects everybody, only federal law applies to climate change.

It’d be a cool argument… if it were supported by a shred of textual evidence. But there’s nothing in the Constitution that makes air pollution an exception to state law (not that the authors of the Constitution had a good understanding of air pollution, which is yet another reason that going back to the original text and intent of the framers is facially stupid, but I digress).

The Clean Air Act seems more directly on point to the issue of air pollution, but Boulder’s lawsuit has a very neat way around that law. Boulder is not suing the energy companies for pollution (which is clearly regulated by the Clean Air Act); it’s suing them for marketing (which is clearly not). It is the marketing of fossil fuels that has abetted climate change and caused damage to Boulder, the city argues, not the production of the fuels themselves.

Kevin Russell, arguing on behalf of Boulder, illustrated this point brilliantly at oral arguments. He said that the companies “can continue to produce as much fossil fuels as they like and contribute to as much air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions as the market will bear, when consumers are properly informed about the consequences of that decision.”

I clapped when Russell said this. I love this argument. But, if we can just speak as adults here, it’s also bullshit. Boulder is absolutely trying to backdoor-regulate greenhouse-gas emissions and the legal sleight of hand here is just that: a magic trick that can’t really obscure what’s going on.

Both Chief Justice Roberts and Kagan were unimpressed with the argument in real time. Kagan immediately followed up Russell’s marketing argument by asking what, if any, limits there would still be on the states to regulate the national and global environment should Boulder prevail.

But making the straight-up preemption argument puts the conservative justices, especially Justice Neil Gorsuch, in a bind. Conservatives generally don’t like federal preemption arguments. That’s because a broad and robust view of federal law that trumps state action can usually be used to put a stop to whatever latest torture Texas or Florida comes up with.

In this case, the only way for the Republican justices to make the energy companies win, now, in the way they want to win, is to take an expansive view of federal preemption and read it into the Constitution or the Clean Air Act where it does not explicitly exist.

Some of the GOP justices are cool with that. Alleged attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh was clear that he thought states have no right to regulate “air and water.” He said there is a “wall of precedents” supporting the idea that only the federal government can act on this issue. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was less strident than Kavanaugh, but she seemed to largely agree with him.

The last interesting wrinkle in the case comes from the fact that the Supreme Court was down a man while debating it. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself from this case, most likely because his wife is thought to own stocks in some of the companies being sued. As a reminder, the state supreme court said that the lawsuit could go forward, so if the Supreme Court justices split, 4–4, the lower court ruling stands and the lawsuit survives.

But I don’t think it will. Federal preemption may be a hard pill for some of the justices to swallow ideologically, but they will take their medicine to prevent Boulder from fighting climate change all by itself. Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson really want the lawsuit to go back to state court (Jackson, to my ears, is the only justice who thinks the lawsuit has a chance of succeeding on the merits), but I think the others will find some way to say federal law doesn’t allow Boulder to do what it’s trying to do. I think Boulder loses at least 6–2, and possibly 8–0 if the liberal justices can join by narrowing the opinion and limiting the damage to environmental rights.

I want Boulder to win precisely because I think Shanmugam is right. I think his Big Oil clients would be eaten alive by state lawsuit after state lawsuit. I think a win here for Boulder could wreck the fossil fuel industry and perhaps force Suncor and ExxonMobil into some kind of settlement or consent decree long before we actually get to the merits of any particular claim for damages.

Which is why the Supreme Court won’t let that happen. It’d be chaos—glorious, righteous chaos. The Republicans on the Supreme Court pretend to not care about the practical effects of their decisions when they make rulings that practically allow children to be shot at school and women to die on gurneys waiting for the lawyers to determine whether they can get an abortion. But they’ll damn sure care about the practical effects of this case.

What’s sad is that the court will care more about the practical effect of climate change lawsuits than the practical effects of climate change.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Reasonable Doubt' You Should Watch Next
description: Stream these other legal dramas—all of them guilty of being addictive viewing.
fullText:
Emayatzy Corinealdi (Middle of Nowhere, The Invitation) is guilty of givign a great performance in the legal drama Reasonable Doubt, now back for its fourth season on Hulu. She plays Jax Stewart, a former public defender now working at a high-powered LA firm, s a self-righteous do-gooder and deeply messy by turns. Jax is not always the most likable character, and she often feels more strongly about her cases than about her actual clients.

For all the show's soapy charms (it comes from Scandal writer Raamla Mohamed), that occasional indifference feels real, as does her complicated personal life. If you're seeking other shows that balance compelling cases with the lawyers' messy lives out of the courtroom, here are 10 shows to stream next.

This David E. Kelley legal thriller (from the Scott Turow bestseller, previously adapted into a movie with Harrison Ford) spends more time in the courtroom than many of these other dramas, which gives it a distinct flavor. Jake Gyllenhaal is Rusty Sabich, a prosecutor charged with investigating the murder of his colleague. His attempts to steer the inquiry land him in hot water when it's discovered that he'd been having an affair with the dead woman—and she was pregnant when she was killed. Rusty quickly becomes the prime suspect, his case not at all helped by his previous shady behavior. The show will be returning for a second season with new lead in Rachel Brosnahan and a new story drawn from the novel Dissection of a Murder by Jo Murray. Stream Presumed Innocent on Apple TV.

A straight reboot of Matlock could've been an easy hit for CBS, but the show pulls a fast one right from the jump: the classic series is just a TV show in the world of Kathy Bates' Maddy Matlock, who just happens to share a name and demeanor with the folksy original—or so we're made to believe, until a bigger plan and longer game are revealed, and we discover that her cute old lady act is just that. She signs on with driven junior partner Olympia Lawrence (Skye P. Marshall), the two alternating between friend and enemy with some all-time great TV chemistry. Stream Matlock on Paramount+.

The legal drama is a durable invention in part because it's so versatile: It can be classy and trashy in equal measure. This one's from Ryan Murphy, which ought to give you some idea of where it falls on that spectrum. The savagely reviewed divorce-centric legal drama was called the worst show of the year—but some of that feels like an anti-All's Fair arms race developed among critics to see who could go the hardest: The Telegraph's Ed Power said it's "a crime against television," The Guardian's Lucy Mangan said of it: "I did not know it was still possible to make television this bad." And yet! Its debut was Hulu's biggest in three years, and viewers kept streaming it, for camp value or otherwise. Good, bad, or gloriously bad, it became one of the year's most talked-about shows, with an A-list cast including Niecy Nash-Betts, Brooke Shields, Teyana Taylor, Sarah Paulson, Judith Light, and Glenn Close. Stream All's Fair on Hulu.

Still one of the juiciest of Shonda Rhimes’ unfailingly juicy shows, How to Get Away With Murder won a number of awards during its run, and is as smart as it is sexy. As the title suggests, it deals more exclusively in murder and conspiracy than Reasonable Doubt, but both shows are anchored by talented, driven lead characters with messy personal lives, constantly navigating the compromises and complexities of the legal system. Here, it's Viola Davis as Annalise Keating, a law professor who, at the show's outset, inadvertently gets five of her most talented students entangled in a murder plot—and things only get more complicated from there. Stream How to Get Away with Murder on Hulu.

A clever and justifiably acclaimed drama, Woo stars Park Eun-bin as an attorney newly hired by a major Seoul law firm. Despite having graduated at the top of her law school class, prejudice made finding work a struggle for the autistic Woo, and much of that follows her into her new workplace. Still, her coworkers (mostly) gradually adapt to her sensory triggers and communication style, made easier by her obvious skill when she's allowed to be herself. With some throughlines that include an office romance, each episode of the show finds Young-woo assigned to a complex case with ties to broader social issues (spousal abuse, governmental corruption, ableism, etc.). A second season is in production. Stream Extraordinary Attorney Woo on Netflix.

This spin-off/sequel to The Good Wife puts the spotlight on Christine Baranski (always a smart move) in her role as Diane Lockhart, on the rocks after a financial scandal involving her goddaughter Maia (Rose Leslie) wipes out her savings and gets her fired. In the aftermath, Diane joins her friend Lucca (Cush Jumbo) at a prestigious Black-owned firm specializing in police brutality cases. The liberal firebrand finds herself at sea not only in her career but in Trump-era America, and the show doesn't shy away from real-life legal and social issues while retaining The Good Wife's tasteful bits of soapy drama. Baranski is joined by the likes of Erica Tazel, Mandy Patinkin, John Larroquette, Audra McDonald, Delroy Lindo, and Alan Cumming, and the show ends on a highly satisfying conclusion to Baranski's 13 years playing Diane. Stream The Good Fight on Paramount+.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama is what solidified her brand—and her spot atop of the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States and also Olivia's lover. This is where Raamla Mohamed, Reasonable Doubt showrunner, cut her teeth as a writer and producer. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Technically a spin-off of The Practice, this occasionally surreal legal drama from David E. Kelley took on ripped-from-the-headlines type legal cases via the legal minds at the high-end (fictional) law firm of Crane, Poole & Schmidt. James Spader is Alan Shore, a lawyer with good intentions but highly questionable methods, who is allied with eccentric and self-obsessed firm partner Denny Crane (William Shatner), in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease yet determined to maintain a virile image. The friendship between the two, despite their wildly opposing perspectives, buoys the legal drama, as does the presence of co-leads Candice Bergen, René Auberjonois, John Larroquette, and Taraji P. Henson. Stream Boston Legal on Hulu.

I always like to sneak in a bit of counter-programming, so here's a legal drama focused on one of the first women lawyers in modern history. A fun and fast-moving crime drama, the show (heavily) dramatizes the live of the real-life Poët, Italy's first female lawyer—disbarred as the series opens in 1883, because LADY LAWYER?! WHAT? While she fights the ruling, she takes a job at her brother's law firm where, of course, she's the real brains of the operation, solving big cases in grand period style (and with a fair bit of sex, as well). Stream The Law According to Lidia Poët on Netflix.

What if a lawyer...but out of the back of a car? Have we done that one yet? Gimmick aside, this is a solid legal drama from genre master David E. Kelley, based on a series of novels from the similarly reliable Michael Connelly. Manuel Garcia-Rulfo stars as Mickey Haller, a recovering addict who inherits the caseload of a murdered colleague. He teams up with Izzy Letts (Jazz Raycole) another recovering addict and former client, to help with cases and to enocourage his sobriety. Meanwhile, he's trying to get joint custody of his daughter with his first ex-wife (Neve Campbell), now a prosecutor, and winds up hiring his second ex-wife (Becki Newton) as a legal aide. You want high-stakes legal drama and messy personal drama? Look no further. Stream The Lincoln Lawyer on Netflix.

title: Davies' 'extra motivation' after Euros heartbreak
description: Defender Mayzee Davies says missing Wales' first major tournament at Euro 2025 with a serious knee injury has given her extra motivation for the World Cup play-offs.
fullText:
Wales defender Mayzee Davies says missing Euro 2025 through injury has given her extra motivation for the World Cup play-offs.

The 20-year-old suffered an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) knee injury on international duty in May 2025 which kept her out of action for 13 months.

She missed Wales' historic first ever major tournament appearance and now is determined to reach the 2027 World Cup.

Wales face Albania in Shkoder on Friday, 9 October in the first leg of their semi-final with the return fixture in Llanelli four days later.

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"It was just so sad for everyone, even in my street, it affected us.

"I'd just broken through [into the team] and I was 18 going to my first major tournament.

"It was horrible, and I think everyone close to me felt it.

"And at the time, I didn't realise how bad it was until I looked back and went how did I get through that?

The Manchester City defender returned to action with Wales for their final two group qualifiers in June against Montenegro and Czech Republic.

And now she is determined not to miss out again.

"I want to get to the World Cup because obviously I missed out last time, so I want to feel what it's like to go to a major tournament with Wales.

"It does give me that extra motivation. I love playing for Wales and I think we're quite a passionate country anyway.

"So I think to play in a World Cup for Wales, obviously in Brazil, it would be amazing.

"Not just for me and my family, obviously coming off the back of the injury as well, I think it would make it extra special if we got there."

Davies admits she found her 13-month recovery tough and worried she may never return.

"I think once I had the surgery I was literally stuck on the sofa, I couldn't do anything on my own.

"I was like, how am I ever going to like be a footballer again at this stage?

"But I had good people around me, team-mates, my family, and then it does get better.

"One day you just wake up and you're like, 'oh, I can start to walk again now'."

Wales have suffered a host of injury withdrawals ahead of the Albania ties, losing a number of key players including Ceri Holland ands Hayley Ladd.

But facing a team 37 places below them in the Fifa world rankings, Davies knows there can be no excuses for Wales as they bid to set up a play-off final against either Romania or Norway.

"Obviously this camp we've had a lot of injuries to like more experienced players, the usual faces," she said.

"But I think everyone in this group now, you have to make sure all the new people feel a part of the team and feel valued.

"She [Head Coach Rhian Wilkinson] said at the end of the day, we always respect every opponent we come up against.

"But this is a must-win game and we can't dwell on who's not here.

"We have to work with who's here now and obviously everyone has their role and we've just got to get the job done."

title: USA will be 'underdogs' in 2027 Ryder Cup - Furyk
description: United States Ryder Cup captain Jim Furyk says his team will be "underdogs" when they attempt to end more than 30 years of pain on European soil in next year's edition at Adare Manor.
fullText:
United States captain Jim Furyk says his team will be "underdogs" when they attempt to end more than 30 years of pain on European soil in next year's Ryder Cup at Adare Manor.

The Americans have not claimed an away Ryder Cup victory since 1993, losing all seven contests in Europe since that victory at The Belfry.

Furyk, who oversaw a 17½-10½ loss to Europe in France in 2018, was handed a second stint as captain earlier this year following Keegan Bradley's team's defeat to Luke Donald's Europe at Bethpage Black in 2025.

"We know what we are up against, we also know it's been 34 years since we won in Europe. There is no secret, I'm going to hear it over and over again so I am going to embrace it," Furyk said during a news conference at Adare Manor in County Limerick.

"Luke and Dodo [Edoardo Molinari, vice-captain] have the opportunity to set the golf course up, tip the scales for Europe. We're the underdogs.

"I know it's always been the Americans who seem to be the favourites, this year there is no chance that could happen. We are the underdogs, we understand that and we have a lot of work ahead of us."

Speaking to BBC Sport NI, Donald said he was not entirely certain about Furyk's assertion that Europe will be favourites in Ireland.

"I think reading between the lines, he is very focused on this Ryder Cup and wants to make amends for what happened in 2018 and the last two Ryder Cups," said Donald.

"He's going to bring a very strong team, that's why I'm not quite so certain that they'll definitely be the underdogs. They'll be strong and will be coming for us but we'll be ready."

Donald, who won four Ryder Cups as a player, led Europe to a resounding 16½-11½ win in Rome in 2023 before masterminding last year's dramatic 15-13 triumph at Bethpage - Europe's first away win since 2012.

The 48-year-old Englishman made just one change to his team for last year's win but he admits there may be more of a "shift" for the centenary edition, having invited potential rookies Eugenio Chacarra, Angel Ayora, Alex Fiztpatrick and Kristoffer Reitan to a scouting trip at Adare Manor last month.

"Certainly something unique was that we had a lot of continuity with the last two teams but I expect that to shift a little bit for this one," added Donald, who is hoping to become the first captain to win three Ryder Cups in a row after victories in Rome and New York.

"There's always new talent coming up, it's about recognising that, getting to know new players, understanding how they tick and coming up with a great plan for success."

In 2018, Jordan Spieth and Justin Thomas - two of the three youngest players on Furyk's team - starred as they won three out of four points as a foursomes and fourballs pairing.

With 21-year-old Jackson Koivun having impressed during an unbeaten Presidents Cup debut in last month's comeback victory over the Internationals in Chicago, Furyk says he is excited to inject more youth into the US side.

"I really love the guys who have played for us in the past few years," the 56-year-old, who played in nine consecutive Ryder Cups between 1997 and 2014, told the BBC.

"We have tough, gritty veterans who have been around the block, and I'm excited, we have a lot of great, young talent who have yet to play in this cup and I'd bet two or three of them will be at Adare."

During the news conference, Furyk said he will ask his team to "do more than any American team has in the past" to seal an elusive away win and vowed to address his side's dismal recent record in foursomes.

The US won just three points from a possible 16 in the alternate-shot format over the past two Ryder Cups.

"I know those numbers very well. I've lived them the last four," said Furyk.

"It's not an anomaly. There's some issues. We understand that. Not something I'm very happy with. I plan on making some changes.

"As captains we need to do a better job – not only putting the folks into good pairings in good positions, but I don't think we are preparing for those matches in a proper way."

The 2027 Ryder Cup - the second to be staged in Ireland after the K Club in 2006 - will take place on 17-19 September.

fullText:
NBA superstar Victor Wembanyama says he was inspired by the unity and camaraderie of rugby after spending part of his summer off-season training with French second tier side Provence.

The 22-year-old Frenchman, who is 7ft 4in and 16st 11lbs, is known for his off-beat search for ways to improve his game. He spent a fortnight focusing on physical and mental strength with Shaolin monks in China in 2025., external

Footage shows Wembanyama, external hitting tackle pads, going through passing drills, taking part in a line-out and looming over the rest of the Provence team in a huddle before a pre-season friendly in August.

He was also filmed sharing a dressing-room embrace with former England international Teimana Harrison, who won five England caps in 2016 and now plays for Provence.

"It was a great experience, seeing the team spirit they have over there," said Wembanyama,, external who was joined on the trip by San Antonio Spurs' team-mate Harrison Barnes.

"It was very inspiring to see the relationship between team-mates, coaches and fans. The training was really hard, really good for stability, movement patterns and developing strength, but I am more grateful for the experience of how I was welcomed there.

"I have never been welcomed anywhere like this. I wasn't part of the team but they treated me like I was. I want to do it again."

Wembanyama combined his work with Provence with hosting his Hoop Gambit event, in which participants play games of chess and basketball, in his hometown of Le Chesnay.

Wembanyama's Spurs fell just short of the NBA Championship earlier this year, going down 4-1 to the New York Knicks in June.

Provence, who previously have been represented by Wales internationals George North and Tomas Francis, have begun their season and search for promotion to the Top 14 well, winning their first five league games.

title: Farbrace leaves Sussex to join Lancashire
description: Lancashire appoint Paul Farbrace as their new director of cricket weeks before he was due to begin the same role at Sussex.
fullText:
Lancashire have appointed Sussex head coach Paul Farbrace as their new director of cricket, weeks before he was due to assume the same role at Hove.

Sussex confirmed in July that Farbrace, 59, would switch roles from head coach to director of cricket from November, where he would work on a part-time basis.

But he now departs to take over from Mark Chilton, who left the post at Old Trafford last month after five years in the job. Farbrace will also oversee the women's team in his new post.

Lancashire finished the season seventh in Division Two of the County Championship, the lowest position in the club's history.

Meanwhile, Farbrace helped guide Sussex to third place in Division One, despite beginning the season with a 12-point penalty.

Lancashire director of cricket Chilton to leave

Farbrace to take up director role at Sussex

What's gone wrong at Lancashire?

The financial problems at Hove which triggered that deduction led Farbace to announce in April that he would step down as head coach at the end of the 2026 season.

In July, he said he would be staying to move into a part-time director of cricket role and oversaw the appointment of Matt Walker as his successor as head coach.

However, the former England assistant coach - who led Sussex to promotion from Division Two in 2024 - has now opted to move to Lancashire.

"It is with mixed emotions that I am leaving Sussex after four years," Farbrace told the club's website, external.

"I will always be grateful to Sussex for giving me the honour of being head coach and allowing me to work with a fabulous group of players and staff."

Farbrace's arrival is the first significant appointment by Lancashire's new chief executive Richard Kenyon, who promised to lead a review of the cricket operation at Emirates Old Trafford.

It is now 11 years since Lancashire won one of cricket's main prizes - the T20 Blast in 2015 - and there has been a nagging feeling amongst the membership that focus had shifted away from the playing side to the commercial side, and also a growing relationship with the Indian backers of the Manchester Super Giants in The Hundred.

But bringing in a person of Farbrace's experience to work above head coach Steven Croft, who has just finished his first full season in the job, is a sign that things are going to be realigned.

Since 2023, Farbrace's first season at Sussex, the Red Rose have won only 11 of their 56 Championship matches, which includes relegation in 2024 and the last two seasons struggling in Division Two.

There was a dire run of nine losses in 10 matches this summer stretching from May to September, as only Gloucestershire kept them off the bottom of the table.

"Paul's credentials and capability for this role were obviously very clear, but he particularly impressed us with his understanding of where the club is and what we need to do to move forward," Kenyon told Lancashire's website, external.

"Paul brings significant experience across both the men's and women's game, as well as an excellent track record of success.

"We wanted an established, high-performing director of cricket, with a strong understanding of the leagues, players and wider landscape of the game - and Paul ticks all those boxes."

The news that Paul Farbrace is leaving Sussex has come completely out of the blue, and will come both as a hammer blow and total shock to everyone at the club.

Farbrace stepped down from his coaching duties at the end of the season, having guided Sussex to a third place finish in the County Championship to take up a new part-time role as director of cricket.

During his four years at the club, Farbrace has steered the club from the bottom of Division Two to promotion, and re-established Sussex as a major force in Division One.

However, with the club still under tight financial controls imposed by the ECB, and with the likes of bowler Henry Crocombe and wicketkeeper John Simpson having already moved on, there are concerns that other players who are out of contract next season may be forced to look for pastures new.

Those concerns will be highlighted by Farbrace's departure. He is immensely popular among the players, staff, supporters, members, as well as the media, and his loss to the club cannot be exaggerated.

fullText:
Martin O'Neill insists he is the man to lead Celtic forward after a "time of reflection" during the ongoing international break.

The 74-year-old signed a one-year deal to stay at Parkhead after two interim spells last season culminated in a league and Scottish Cup double.

Following two defeats by Rangers last month - either side of a 3-1 home defeat by Ferencvaros in the Europa League - O'Neill said "it might be time to wrap it up", in reference to his managerial career.

However, Celtic rallied around their legendary boss, with chief executive Michael Nicholson publicly backing the Northern Irishman.

And two weeks on, O'Neill himself has now stated he has the drive to stay on.

"I am extremely prepared now for it," O'Neill said in a club interview. "We had a difficult week. That can happen. You can lose to your arch-rivals, you can lose the European game.

"It's certainly not the end of the world as it seemed to be described as. I thought I would take a bit of time, and it didn't take me that much time to think about it.

"I want to lead the club, I want to try to win the league and I'm just as determined now than ever before.

"It was a time of reflection for a moment or two, but overall, I'm back, I'm raring to go and the team's ready."

title: 'Means more than just a trophy' - Djokovic claims 102nd title of career
description: Novak Djokovic claims the 102nd title of his astonishing career as Alex de Minaur retires injured from the China Open final.
fullText:
Novak Djokovic claimed the 102nd title of his astonishing career as Alex de Minaur retired injured from the China Open final.

The 39-year-old led De Minaur - a player 12 years his junior - 7-6 (7-3) 0-1 when the Australian was forced to quit with an apparent left thigh problem.

Both players took a medical timeout after a 68-minute first set, but De Minaur managed just one game on their return before shaking hands.

It is the 21st year in a row that Djokovic has won at least one singles title.

Only Jimmy Connors (109) and Roger Federer (103) have won more singles titles in their careers than the Serb.

Djokovic is on a 34-match winning streak at the China Open, having claimed the trophy seven times.

"I always have high expectations and want to visualise myself with the trophy, but particularly here in Beijing, the place where I've never lost," Djokovic said.

"This trophy means much more than one trophy, one tournament."

The 24-time Grand Slam champion was competing in only his second final of the year after losing January's Australian Open showpiece to Carlos Alcaraz.

Djokovic beat world number two Alexander Zverev on his way to the Beijing final and was a set and a break up on third seed Daniil Medvedev when the Russian was defaulted from their semi-final.

Djokovic's ability to compete at the highest level is rarely in question - he beat world number one Sinner to reach the Australian Open final and took a set off Alcaraz in the showpiece - but his body has let him down in recent years.

He was left in tears following a gruelling first-round loss at the US Open and spoke about struggling with a "serious health condition" that particularly bothered him in oppressive conditions.

He reached the semi-finals of Wimbledon, losing to eventual champion Jannik Sinner, but suffered a surprise third-round exit at the French Open at the hands of rising star Joao Fonseca.

This is Djokovic's first title in just over a year, having limited his schedule to protect his body.

Victory will also see him return to inside the world's top 10.

"This year has been quite challenging for me, lots of ups and downs and physical and health issues, so I was just trying to find a good feeling on the court," Djokovic said.

"I know that when I'm feeling well and striking the ball well I can still compete at the highest level.

"This week has been an evidence to that. I'm very proud."

Earlier, Alcaraz won the Japan Open, claiming a trophy in just his third tournament since injuring his wrist in April.

The Spaniard came back from an early break down to beat Czech Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4) 6-4 and successfully defend his title in Tokyo.

Alcaraz only returned to competitive tennis at August's US Open, where he reached the quarter-finals before losing in five tight sets to Ben Shelton.

It is Alcaraz's third title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January to complete the career Grand Slam, and also February's Qatar Open.

"It's extra special after my injury," the 25-year-old said.

"It was a tough week that I didn't find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find the good solutions.

"I think that's what matters in the end."

title: Rival clubs want retrospective and future punishments for Man City
description: A number of Premier League clubs want Manchester City to be hit with both retrospective punishments and sanctions in the future.
fullText:
A number of Premier League clubs want Manchester City to be hit with both "retrospective punishments" and sanctions for the future for their mass financial rule-breaking, sources have told BBC Sport.

An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have appealed against the verdict, while the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) is poised to look at the findings to see if there may be any suggestions of potential misconduct.

However, there is said to be a consensus among a group of top-flight club executives that if City's appeal is unsuccessful, the sanctions should make reparations for the period when they broke the rules, while also limiting their powers in future.

There is also a feeling from at least four Premier League boardrooms that a "one-hit" points deduction resulting in relegation to the Championship would be an insufficient punishment given the severity of City's wrongdoing.

There is understood to be nuance in exactly what clubs consider a fitting penalty for the eight-time Premier League champions, who were found guilty of all serious financial rule breaches in a damning verdict by an independent commission.

One senior club source said City should be stripped of their titles, and added there was "no great rush" among clubs to push for the redistribution of trophies, but rather to take honours away and leave them vacant.

The source warned the credibility of the Premier League would be lost if City were allowed to keep the eight major trophies they won during the period they have been found guilty.

However, in a sign of a range of opinions across the league, BBC Sport was previously told there was little appetite among other clubs for City to be stripped of titles.

Regarding the timescale for sanctions in the future, there is a concern among club executives that a sanction applied just to one season would merely provide City with a "bump in the road" given the likelihood of them returning to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

A number of Premier League figures therefore believe any points deduction should be split over multiple seasons, while there is also a sense that transfer bans that stretch over a number of windows would also significantly hinder City's ability to regain their top-flight status as quickly as possible.

Which clubs did Man City's 'inflated' money flow to in transfer market?

Man City whistleblower to lose witness protection

One club source also said it would be "bizarre, almost obtuse" if City were able to trade in the upcoming January transfer window, if this process is ongoing and sanctions have not been applied.

Some clubs cited feeling "in the dark" regards the Premier League, including around the chronology and timescales of the appeal and the sanctions hearing.

However, sources said there was "empathy" and "understanding" about the difficult position the Premier League is in, given the gravity of this situation and the ongoing legal process.

Regarding financial reparations, one idea that has been mooted - and which a club source found "merit" in - was to apply a "tariff-based system", whereby City's past league finishing positions would be altered via a points deduction.

Rival clubs could then be paid compensation by City based on where they would have finished versus where they did finish.

BBC Sport understands Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca will speak to players collectively after they arrive back from international duty on Thursday, before their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday (16:30 BST).

The trip to Anfield is their first game since news of the verdict broke.

Merseyside Police says it has received queries in relation to the match, and when asked by BBC Sport if any special measures would be put in place the force said it will have "an appropriate policing operation in place on the day".

Sources at Liverpool have told BBC Sport it is a case of "business as usual" and there are no extra measures being put in place. Conversations and meetings between the club, supporters and relevant authorities take place before every home game.

One source said while everyone "has the right to express their feelings" they hoped supporters would not overstep the mark.

title: Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge Jesus "broke his word to me".
fullText:
Cristiano Ronaldo says he is not retiring from international football but deserves to be punished for walking out on Portugal after head coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word".

The 41-year-old captain left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.

Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.

In a lengthy statement, external, which ran to nearly 2,000 words, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player said he should be held accountable for his actions.

But he accused Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media.

"The Portuguese Football Federation must assess the consequences of my actions and punish me for them. I believe the punishment should not be reduced," Ronaldo said.

"I have already apologised, but I know that actions have consequences."

Ronaldo's statement comes after Portugal head coach Jesus said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.

Jesus said on Sunday that the door was still open for Ronaldo to play for the country's national team.

Ronaldo said that, provided he was "physically fit, playing with my team, and hopefully scoring goals", he would like to continue to play international football.

"After my suspension period ends, I will be available, as I always have been, to compete and win with our national team," he added.

BBC Sport has approached the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) for comment.

Ronaldo's statement struck a conciliatory tone in places, but he was also critical of Portugal coach Jesus as he provided his version of the dispute which prompted him to walk out on the squad last week.

He said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness.

However, on the day of the Norway game, the 72-year-old coach told him he would play for 30 minutes.

"Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said.

"The manager had broken his word to me."

A later meeting with Jesus produced an agreement for the coach to clarify matters at his next news conference.

Ronaldo said an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus' decisions and that the coach asking "someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona" to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake.

Portugal's record appearance holder said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him but said the coach's public remarks did not reflect their private discussion.

"The conference was what is known: the attitude had nothing to do with our meeting," Ronaldo explained.

"I heard expressions and an aggressiveness I believe I did not deserve, a "High and mighty" attitude that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before."

Ronaldo said it was the "second time" Jesus had "broken his word to me" and he decided to leave the training camp "without waiting for any further broken promises".

Prior to his appointment as head coach, Ronaldo said he had described Jesus - who had previously managed him at Al Nassr - as the "right choice".

Ronaldo had considered retiring from international football after this summer's World Cup - at which Portugal exited at the last-16 stage - and said he had written a letter to fans containing the words he wanted to tell them when he announced it, but he was urged to reconsider by the FPF's president, Pedro Proenca, on the flight home from the United States.

Ronaldo's behaviour drew contrasting opinions in his homeland with Jesus getting some support in the media and among fans at odds with those loyal to legendary player.

Ronaldo said that, despite the "absolute breakdown of trust" in Jesus' word, he should not have left and the "responsibility is mine alone", as he said sorry to his fellow players and Portugal's supporters.

He added: "I owe an apology to my national team teammates for having left the camp... I apologise to the Portuguese people once again, but a broken word has, for me, a defining impact."

Ronaldo's search for a record 1,000 career goals continues and he has returned to training in Saudi Arabia with Al-Nassr.

He has scored 979 times for Portugal, Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al-Nassr.

Portugal won the matches against Norway and Denmark without Ronaldo in the side, and are back in action in November in their final Nations League group games against the Danes and Wales.

title: Mikaela Shiffrin, the slalom skiing GOAT, to focus on other disciplines this season
description: First, some facts: Mikaela Shiffrin is the greatest Alpine skier in the history of the sport. She is far and away the greatest slalom skier in the history of the sport. No one is even close on that one. She is 31 years old. She’s 15 seasons into her career.
fullText:
Mikaela Shiffrin is the greatest Alpine skier in the history of the sport. She is far and away the greatest slalom skier in the history of the sport. No one is even close on that one.

She is 31 years old. She's 15 seasons into her career. She has way more races behind her than ahead of her. It's the point in the career of an elite athlete when they generally focus on what they do best.

It's about the age when Roger Federer started dialing back on clay-court tournaments to better prepare for the grass. It's the time of a career when a great slugger in baseball shows up in the field less and spends more time as the designated hitter. It's when Katie Ledecky raced more of the longest races in the pool instead of the shorter ones, when Michael Phelps stopped doing the 400-meter individual medley so he could focus mostly on butterfly and freestyle.

So, Shiffrin being Shiffrin, she did the opposite of all that. The winningest slalom skier that anyone could ever have imagined, a two-time Olympic gold medalist and nine-time winner of the season-long championship in slalom announced Tuesday morning on her podcast, "What's the Point," that she was going to dial way back on her specialty.

She will ski a couple of slalom races — enough, she hopes, to maintain her starting position amid the best skiers on the World Cup circuit next season. She will skip the season-opening slalom races in Finland and Austria at the start of the season next month but race slalom in Killington, Vermont, later in November. She will sprinkle in a couple more slalom races after that, depending on her results. As of now, though, she does not plan to ski much more slalom than that.

The woman who crashed so hard in giant slalom two years ago that she battled post-traumatic stress disorder when she faced the prospect of skiing the faster races with fewer turns, wants to live with that fear and embrace the speed.

She knows she is likely to win far less often. She may not win at all. That's fine.

"What has changed is not my respect or love for slalom," Shiffrin explained on her podcast. "It's where I feel curious enough to put in the enormous amount of work that it takes to challenge the fastest racers in the world. For a really long time, most of my curiosity pulled me toward that process in slalom.

"I loved doing thousands and thousands of turns, obsessing over every tiny detail, sharpening that reaction speed and trying to find even one more hundredth. I even loved the way the event made my body hurt.

"Right now, I feel more excited about World Cup races. Putting that energy into (giant slalom) and super-G."

It's worth noting that Shiffrin is plenty good at giant slalom and super-G. She has won more giant slalom World Cup races (22) than any other woman and won the 2019 and 2023 season titles in the discipline. In 2019, she won the season title in super-G.

For the better part of seven months, ever since Shiffrin claimed another Olympic slalom gold medal in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy, the question of what could possibly be next for the sport's biggest star has floated around winter sports circles. For two months, it pinged around Shiffrin's brain, too.

She'd won just about everything there was to win, including a silly 110 World Cup races — the most in history, men or women, and 24 more than second-place — plus three Olympic gold medals and a silver. In Cortina, she exorcised the ghost of the 2022 Olympics in Beijing, when she struggled to finish events, crashing three times and coming away from the Games with no medals out of six events.

She was engaged. She'd been chasing after this one thing for about 25 years, or more than 80 percent of her life. Had she announced her retirement, no one would have begrudged her.

When the season ended, Shiffrin huddled with her fiancé, Aleksander Aamodt Kilde, the Norwegian skiing champion, and those closest to her, and went through every permutation of what her future might look like. She wants to have a family of her own eventually. But she does have more skiing to do first. Maybe it will last through the 2030 Olympics in the French Alps. Maybe it won't. For now, the ski racing will be season by season.

But what kind of ski racing, and why?

Shiffrin is a deep thinker, asking herself and those around her all the big questions, even the existential ones, like, "What's the point?"

It's not the best quality for elite athletes, who often perform best with a quiet mind. For a ski racer who occasionally flies down an icy slope at nearly 80 mph, "What's the point?" isn't all that useful a question.

But Shiffrin had to ask it. And the answers had to do with caring and longevity, and the interplay of the two.

Slalom beats the hell out of her body. It requires endless precision training and an immeasurable headspace. Less of it would create more opportunity.

"I can look at shifting my program as stepping away from something, or I can look at it as creating room to keep doing this thing that I love a bit longer," she said. "That's how I'm thinking about it. I'm not trying to do less because I care less. I'm trying something different because I still care a lot."

In early spring, when offseason training schedules get formulated, Shiffrin delivered the news to her coaches and the rest of her team.

"I was like, 'Right on, let's go,'" her lead coach, Karin Harjo, said in an interview Monday. "The joy that she gets in the challenge and improving and getting better, when you know that about her and you work with her closely, then it makes complete sense. That was my initial reaction right away. I was like, 'Sweet, let's do that. Let's go forward.'"

Shiffrin has not trained in slalom at all this offseason. She went to Mammoth Mountain in California to train with the U.S. speed team in May, focusing on super-G and some giant slalom as well. She focused on giant slalom at another spring camp at Copper Mountain, Colorado, alongside the women's speed team. She trained in Chile, as she almost always does during the summer, but it's been different.

No longer is she doing all those slalom turns and squeezing in giant slalom and super-G when she can.

"When you're not chasing three, four disciplines, it does give you a lot more ability to kind of focus and have these longer focus blocks," Harjo said. "Like anything, when you spread yourself a little bit thinner, the more you do it, it has a different feel to it. It's not necessarily lower quality, but it's definitely more taxing on the body, for sure."

It's not that skiing faster isn't plenty taxing. It is, especially when spills happen. But the tighter turns of slalom exert more gravitational force on the body. Also, slalom skiers smack more than 50 plastic gates at roughly 40 mph on every run. That starts to hurt after a while.

The longer radius of a turn in giant slalom, and the gliding runs of super-G have far less pull and fewer collisions with gates. But there is the speed, and the fear factor.

Harjo said Shiffrin has embraced that. Just because she might be afraid of something doesn't mean she can't do it.

"Her response says, 'OK, this is a cool challenge to figure out," Harjo said of Shiffrin. "Having fear doesn't mean it has to hold you back."

And so, as Shiffrin begins her 16th season of World Cup races, she has found a way to do something new, something different, something uncomfortable and, for now, exciting. It's got nothing to do with slalom not being challenging, or that she is done with that. She isn't. She'll go hard with slalom training before the races.

For now though, the focus is somewhere else, on a different question. It's not about how much she can squeeze into one season. It's about what happens if she gives herself enough space to follow her curious mind.

"I don't actually know the answer," she said. "That's kind of the point."

title: Argentina vs. Benin start time, how to watch as Lionel Messi says farewell

Argentina will play Benin in a friendly at Estadio Monumental, but the actual match will be a sideshow compared to the spectacle of the legendary figure's final international game.

Messi announced his international retirement in August, but Argentina has called the 39-year-old up one final time to get a send-off in front of his home fans.

"I want to tell you that after a chat we had with the manager of the national team, Lionel Scaloni, we've made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the emblem of our national team, our captain Lionel Andres Messi so he is able to have the goodbye he really deserves on Oct. 6 here in Argentina," Argentina Football Association  president Claudio "Chiqui" Tapia said last month.

"It's going to be an unforgettable day for everyone. Everyone wants to be at this match, and now it's just about enjoying it," Scaloni said.

title: BYU's Kihei Akina is halfway to a PGA Tour card after top 10 in Utah
description: BYU sophomore Kihei Akina earned two points toward his PGA Tour card after a top-10 finish in Utah.
fullText:
Kihei Akina is halfway to earning a PGA Tour card.

The sophomore at BYU finished ninth Sunday at the PGA Tour's Bank of Utah Championship. This was his third start in the championship and his first time playing the weekend, and it paid off in a big way.

Akina, the reigning Phil Mickelson Award winner as college golf's Freshman of the Year, earned two points toward his PGA Tour University Accelerated total, putting him at 10. That means he needs 10 more to earn a PGA Tour card.

"Just a great week to be back here in Utah again," Akina said. "Just really lucky to have the privilege to be able to play here for the third time, and to be able to play well, it's pretty awesome."

Akina, who was born in Hawaii and played high school golf in Utah before committing to BYU, has risen to 10th in the World Amateur Golf Ranking. He was a member of the U.S. Walker Cup team last month and had zero Accelerated points when the year began.

He has made three cuts on the PGA Tour this year. He finished top 10 at the NCAA Men's Golf Championship in June, played on the Palmer and Walker Cup teams and now has a top-10 finish on Tour. That's how he got to 10 points, and only one player, Texas Tech junior Connor Graham, has more Accelerated points. Tennessee freshman Tyler Watts also has 10 points.

With his top-10 finish in Utah, Akina also earned a spot in the field for the Butterfield Bermuda Championship later this month at Port Royal in Southampton. Another made cut and top 10 there would be worth two points.

Three players – Gordon Sargent, Luke Clanton and Jackson Koivun – have earned their PGA Tour cards via Accelerated. Akina is looking to become the fourth, and if his trajectory continues as it has in 2026, he could be there by year's end.

"It's in the back of your head," Akina said. "At the end of the day, you've just got to play golf, and that's what I did this week."

Cameron Jourdan is an assistant editor of Golfweek, covering college and amateur golf, the PGA Tour and plenty more. Follow Cameron on X/Twitter (@Cam_Jourdan) or Instagram (@GolfweekJourdan).

title: Latest bowl projection has Duke facing SEC power
description: Duke is hoping to reach its fifth straight bowl game for the first time in program history.
fullText:
At 4-0, and with the season in a conference that has turned into Miami and everyone else, Duke's hopes of reaching the conference title game for the second year and getting a chance to repeat are improving every week.

And while a spot in the College Football Playoff is still an outside chance, Manny Diaz is two wins away from leading the Blue Devils to a fifth straight bowl game for the first time in program history.

SI.com's Bryan Fischer released his latest bowl projections and has Duke in an interesting matchup against SEC powerhouse Tennessee in the Gator Bowl on Dec. 30 in Jacksonville, Fla.

The Volunteers are 4-1, with their only loss coming to top-ranked Texas. For an SEC schedule, Tennessee has it pretty good heading into the second half of the season, facing only two ranked opponents in Alabama and LSU. The Vols have been stingy on defense but have struggled to find consistent quarterback play.

Duke and Tennessee have met 19 times previously, with the Vols holding a slim 14-13-2 lead.

title: McClean hits out at 'incomprehensible' Derry treatment
description: Derry City player James McClean hits out at his treatment by Derry City amid an ongoing contract dispute with the club.
fullText:
James McClean says he cannot "understand or accept" how he has been treated by Derry City amid an ongoing contract dispute with the club.

In a statement released on the Professional Footballers' Association of Ireland (PFAI) website, the former Republic of Ireland international describes attempts by the League of Ireland club to terminate his contract as "incomprehensible" and says he will decide himself when is the right time to retire.

The 37-year-old insists he is still fit and available to play "when called upon" despite being left out of the squad by interim manager Mark Connolly.

McClean did apologise for some "misjudged" actions on his part over recent months, adding that "his frustrations should have remained in-house".

He returned to his hometown club from Wrexham in the close-season in January but has not been included in a match-day squad since the Candystripes' Uefa Conference League defeat by Rijeka in early July.

Reports have indicated in recent months that Derry attempted to terminate McClean's contract because of persistent injuries, a matter alluded to in Tuesday's statement by the PFAI.

The statement says that Derry had attempted to invoke Section 18 of the Standard Players Contract, which permits them to terminate a contract with six months' notice when a player is deemed to have a "permanent incapacity", as confirmed by an independent physician.

"For any club to feel it is OK to attempt to terminate a player's contract without any due process or just cause is incomprehensible, and it sets a dangerous precedent for every player in this league," said McClean.

"I am not permanently incapacitated, or anything even remotely close to that. I am capable of contributing and doing well in the League of Ireland. I train as hard and give as much as anyone."

"I will decide when I retire. Nobody else will make that decision for me. When that time comes, my body will tell me. This is my life and my career. I deserve the same duty of care and fairness given to the majority of other players at Derry City FC."

The PFAI gave further information on the nature and extent of the player's injury.

"In short, James has had a hip injury which had been causing intermittent issues for him. This has caused him to miss some games and occasional training sessions," the statement read.

"He has sought medical treatment for this and is currently fit and well.

"He has trained fully for the last nine weeks and has made himself available for selection. He recently played in an internal match arranged by the club. He believes he can help the team and has not been provided with a satisfactory reason for being left out of the squad."

BBC Sport NI contacted Derry City for comment but a spokesperson said that the club were presently "solely focused on this weekend's FAI Cup semi-final against Galway United (Saturday, 15:00 BST kick-off).

title: Oscar De La Hoya Sparks Fresh Boxing Tension With “Second Class” Claim After Ryan Garcia Win
description: Oscar De La Hoya has sparked a fresh debate in boxing after calling British boxing “second class” compared with the […]
fullText:
Oscar De La Hoya has sparked a fresh debate in boxing after calling British boxing "second class" compared with the United States following Ryan Garcia's stoppage win over Conor Benn.

The Golden Boy Promotions founder made the comments on The Ariel Helwani Show in early October, about three weeks after Garcia stopped Benn in the second round in Las Vegas. De La Hoya praised boxing's size and popularity in the United Kingdom but questioned whether British fighters get the development needed to compete with the best American fighters.

His comments drew attention because Benn entered the fight unbeaten in 26 professional bouts and was challenging for a world title for the first time. Garcia's win ended that run and fueled an old debate about the strength of British boxing.

De La Hoya said he respects boxing's popularity in Britain but believes fighter development doesn't match what happens in the United States.

"I love the fact that boxing is huge in the UK… but the fighters are not really developing to that championship level," De La Hoya said. "Once you come to the U.S. and fight the real talent, then you see the reality of UK boxing. It's subpar, it's second class to U.S. boxing."

His comments came after Garcia stopped Benn at T-Mobile Arena on September 12. Garcia dropped Benn with a right hand early in the second round before referee Thomas Taylor stopped the fight at 1:25.

Garcia improved to 26-2 and retained his WBC welterweight title. He also called for a unification fight with Teofimo Lopez after the victory.

The Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn fight drew a sold-out crowd of nearly 19,000, with reports putting the gate above $8 million. Garcia used his speed and left hook early, then took advantage when Benn moved forward.

Benn entered the fight after returning to the 147-pound welterweight limit for the first time in more than four years. He had previously competed at middleweight and light-middleweight.

The loss was Benn's first stoppage defeat in 27 professional fights and his first world-title challenge. His trainer, Tony Sims, later said Benn would not return to welterweight because making the weight had been difficult despite the financial reward.

Benn was taken to hospital for examination after the stoppage. He has since indicated that he plans to regroup at a higher weight.

De La Hoya's comments on British boxing have reopened a long-running debate over how fighters are developed and tested before reaching the world stage. He pointed to differences in talent pipelines, sparring and the level of opposition fighters face before major international fights.

The comments also sparked a divided reaction on social media. Some fans pointed to Britain's history of producing world champions across several weight classes. Others argued that Benn had faced tougher opposition than he usually encountered before meeting Garcia.

The aftermath of the fight also brought tension between Garcia and De La Hoya. Garcia expressed disappointment that De La Hoya was not ringside and did not walk him to the ring, despite reportedly having a seat available.

The Garcia-Benn result offers one clear example for De La Hoya's argument, but it does not settle the wider debate. British boxing continues to produce world champions, while American boxing remains a major center for elite fighters and international matchups.

title: OpenAI has ‘work to do to rebuild trust’ in Australia, executive tells AI inquiry
description: Anthropic tells inquiry it ‘never tried to dictate’ Australian copyright rules as the ABC says copyright laws do not need...
fullText:
Anthropic tells inquiry it ‘never tried to dictate’ Australian copyright rules as the ABC says copyright laws do not need changing

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI has used an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry on AI to apologise again to Australia about the hack on Medicare last month, as media and entertainment organisations argued weakening copyright law for AI model training would leave artists as “roadkill”.

Meanwhile Anthropic told the inquiry it was not seeking to dictate copyright law on model training, but the current rules made it “impossible” to train AI in Australia.

Tuesday morning’s hearing of the joint parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence largely focused on copyright licensing for AI training in Australia, amid concerns companies such as Anthropic were pushing the Australian government to adopt an opt-out model, requiring rights holders to specifically opt out of allowing AI to train on their content.

Anthropic’s special envoy, the former US ambassador to Australia Jeffrey Bleich, told the committee that Anthropic had “never tried to dictate to Australia” on copyright.

“We’ve just shared information about how the training works, and then discussed what its implications would be with respect to our capacity to operate here,” he said.

Anthropic suggests current Australian laws mean AI companies need to obtain a licence for the use of every piece of content on the internet as training material. Bleich said this was “technically impossible”.

Anthropic was keen to explore what the Australian government wants to do to incentivise training in Australia, and Bleich said Australia could shape frontier models if they were trained here, otherwise it would ultimately rely on models trained elsewhere.

OpenAI apologised for its AI agents attacking a number of Australian government websites in June. The multibillion-dollar company notified the government via an email to a public-facing address three months after the breach.

“I want to begin with an apology. During internal training and evaluation, our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to. That should not have happened. We also should have handled our response better,” OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, told the committee on Tuesday afternoon.

“We are sorry, and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people. We are committed to doing that work.”

Following the revelation of a separate hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service last week, Kwon told the committee OpenAI was reviewing logs of AI agent training dating back to November 2025, which identified the latest hack activity taking place in June.

He promised that should more incidents be identified, government agencies would be notified “very, very quickly”.

OpenAI representatives, while apologetic, downplayed the agent activity on Australian government websites as not “not super sophisticated” compared with the Hugging Face attack. The independent senator David Pocock questioned why the company didn’t contact ministers, instead sending an email “to some arbitrary department email” after the Medicare incident.

“I think that on retrospect, we should have done what you were suggesting … I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation, and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties – but it’s not good enough,” Kwan said.

Anthropic’s head of safeguards, Dave Orr, told the committee the company had reviewed hundreds of millions of transcripts of its models and had not found any cases in which it interacted with Australian government systems in an unauthorised way.

He could not say whether Anthropic’s customers may have used the models on Australian government systems, given the company’s “zero data retention” policy.

Annabelle Herd, the chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), told the committee that “Australia’s artists will be the roadkill in the rush” to make deals with AI companies, and said Aria was not against AI frontier model training being done in Australia but it should be done on “our terms”.

“There is nothing less sovereign than rewriting our laws to suit foreign company commercial interests, done the way that big AI is proposing,” she said. “It will devastate the music industry and make Australia a pariah for rights holders globally.”

She said Anthropic and OpenAI were “asking the government for a free ride” and the creative sector was calling on the government not to cave in to their demands.

The ABC told the committee Australia’s existing copyright regime was “completely adequate”.

The ABC’s head of content and legal operations, Kate Gilchrist, said an opt-out system as proposed by AI companies would place burdens and costs on rights holders, as it would require ongoing surveillance to see whether copyright material was being used.

She said for the ABC, it would mean ensuring every site on which the ABC publishes material had opted out.

“We cannot scour the internet and ensure we are opting out on all of those different sites of publication. It simply does not work,” she said.

Gilchrist said she suspected ABC content had been scraped already.

The union representing the entertainment and news sector, the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), has called for an equitable remuneration scheme that would put fees on companies across the AI technology stack.

“Revenue would support two things: direct payments to creative and media workers whose work contributes to AI systems. And secondly, a cultural fund supporting Australian live entertainment, screen music, public interest journalism and cultural activity,” the MEAA’s acting chief executive, Adam Portelli, said.

The committee is holding hearings from Tuesday to Friday this week.
